title: World Court to rule today on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya
summary: The International Court of Justice delivers its judgment on Thursday in The Gambia's seven-year case against Myanmar, in what would be the first time the court has ever found a state responsible for genocide.
content: The International Court of Justice will deliver its judgment on Thursday, November 19, on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya, closing a case that has run for seven years and could make legal history. Judges at the Peace Palace in The Hague will begin reading the ruling at 10 a.m. local time, in a case brought by The Gambia in November 2019 under the 1948 Genocide Convention. The case concerns the military crackdown in Myanmar's Rakhine State in August 2017, when security forces launched what they called clearance operations after attacks by Rohingya insurgents on police posts. More than 740,000 Rohingya fled across the border into Bangladesh in the weeks that followed, according to [figures cited by Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2026/11/18/icj-to-rule-on-rohingya-genocide-case-what-to-expect), joining hundreds of thousands who had already fled earlier waves of violence. More than one million Rohingya now live in refugee camps in Bangladesh, most of them in Cox's Bazar, one of the largest refugee settlements in the world. The Gambia, acting with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation, argues that the 2017 offensive and the treatment of the Rohingya before and after it breached the Genocide Convention, the treaty adopted in 1948 that obliges states to prevent and punish the destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. Myanmar denies the charge. Its lawyers have told the court the operations were a legitimate counter-terrorism campaign, not an attempt to destroy the Rohingya as a people. At the centre of the case is intent. To find genocide, the court must be satisfied not only that killings, serious bodily harm and the infliction of destructive conditions took place, but that they were carried out with the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya group, in whole or in part. That requirement has been the main obstacle in earlier genocide cases before the court, and legal experts quoted in the run-up to the judgment have described it as the hardest question the judges must answer. The stakes go beyond Myanmar. Since it began operating in 1946, the International Court of Justice has never found a state responsible for genocide. Thursday's ruling will be only the third genocide judgment the court has ever delivered, and its first in more than a decade. A finding against Myanmar would make it the first state ever held responsible for genocide under the 1948 Convention. The case reached its merits hearings in January 2026, after the court rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections to its jurisdiction and to the admissibility of the application in 2022. The judgment is final and cannot be appealed. Myanmar is legally bound to follow it, but the court has no police force and no means of enforcing its decisions. If Myanmar ignores an adverse ruling, The Gambia can ask the UN Security Council to act, a route that runs into the veto power of its permanent members, including China and Russia, both of which have shielded Myanmar diplomatically in the past. The run-up to the ruling has also been shadowed by pressure on the court itself. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a Washington think tank described as close to the White House, has predicted that a genocide finding would lead the United States to sanction the court. The United States has already sanctioned judges of the International Criminal Court after it issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and it has sanctioned the ICC as an institution. Fears have focused in particular on Navi Pillay, the former UN human rights chief chosen by The Gambia as its ad hoc judge in the case, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in October for her work promoting international law and accountability. Whatever the court decides, the judgment will not by itself resolve the Rohingya's displacement or determine who governs Rakhine State. The Arakan Army, an ethnic armed group, now controls large areas of Rakhine, while Myanmar's military authorities have rejected a proposal from Bangladesh's Jamaat-e-Islami for an independent Rohingya state. For the refugees in Bangladesh, the ruling is about recognition and the possibility of a lawful route home, but the camps are likely to remain their home for years to come, whatever the judges say on Thursday. The ruling is also expected to shape how lawyers and governments read the court's other pending genocide cases, including Ukraine's case against Russia, the Democratic Republic of Congo's case against Rwanda, and South Africa's case against Israel over Gaza. Each turns on the same difficult question of intent, and each will now be argued in the shadow of what the judges say about Myanmar. The United States already classifies the Rohingya crisis as genocide, on the basis of a determination by the Biden administration. The ruling comes on the same day that [the leaders of the United States, China and Russia meet in Shenzhen](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19) for their first trilateral summit, a reminder of how much of the world's diplomacy now runs through courts and summits at the same time. [Reuters reported](https://news.az/news/world-court-announces-date-for-rohingya-genocide-ruling) that the court announced the November 19 date on November 3, giving survivors, governments and lawyers just over two weeks to prepare for a decision many have awaited since The Gambia filed its case. For the Rohingya in the camps of Cox's Bazar, Thursday morning will be the moment seven years of waiting finally produces an answer.
